tools.name: netobserv_export_flows
tools.description: Exports NetObserv flow records as CSV with the same filters as list_flows. Use when the user needs downloadable flow data for audits or offline analysis.

columns.description: Optional comma-separated column names to include (e.g. SrcK8S_Namespace,DstK8S_Namespace,Bytes). Omit to export all columns present in the result.

endTime.description: End of time range as Unix epoch seconds. Defaults to now.

filters.description:
NetObserv filter expression passed to the console plugin (plain text; the client URL-encodes it).

Syntax:
- key=value — exact match; key=a,b — OR multiple values for the same key
- key~pattern — regex / contains match; key!~pattern — NOT regex
- key!=value — not equal; key>number — numeric greater-or-equal (e.g. Bytes>1000)
- AND within a group: & (e.g. SrcK8S_Namespace=default&Proto=6)
- OR between groups: | (e.g. SrcK8S_Name=pod-a|SrcK8S_Name=pod-b)

Prefer the dedicated "namespace" parameter for namespace scope when possible.
Use Kubernetes list tools (namespaces, pods, deployments, etc.) to discover filter values.

Common Kubernetes fields (Src/Dst prefixes mirror each other):
- SrcK8S_Namespace, DstK8S_Namespace, SrcK8S_Name, DstK8S_Name
- SrcK8S_Type, DstK8S_Type (e.g. Pod, Service, Node)
- SrcK8S_OwnerName, DstK8S_OwnerName, SrcK8S_OwnerType, DstK8S_OwnerType (for Deployment, StatefulSet, etc.)
- SrcK8S_HostName, DstK8S_HostName, SrcK8S_Zone, DstK8S_Zone, K8S_ClusterName, UDN

Network & flow:
- SrcAddr, DstAddr (IPs), SrcPort, DstPort, Proto (IANA number, e.g. 6=TCP, 17=UDP)
- FlowDirection (0=Ingress, 1=Egress, 2=Inner), Bytes, Packets, Dscp, Flags

Packet drops (often with recordType flowLog and packetLoss dropped/hasDrops):
- PktDropPackets, PktDropBytes, PktDropLatestState, PktDropLatestDropCause

DNS:
- DnsName, DnsId, DnsLatencyMs, DnsErrno, DnsFlagsResponseCode

Examples:
- SrcK8S_Namespace=openshift-netobserv&SrcK8S_Name~my-app
- Proto=6&DstPort=443
- SrcK8S_Name=pod-a|SrcK8S_Name=pod-b

format.description: Export format. Only csv is supported.

limit.description: Maximum number of flow records to return. Default 100.

namespace.description: Restrict results to flows where source or destination namespace matches (dev-scoped Loki tenant).

startTime.description: Start of time range as Unix epoch seconds. Overrides timeRange when set.

timeRange.description: Lookback window in seconds when startTime is omitted. Default 300.

tools.name: netobserv_get_flow_metrics
tools.description: Returns aggregated NetObserv flow metrics as topology or time-series data. Use for throughput, TLS/DNS/drop breakdowns, and namespace or workload traffic analysis; see aggregateBy and groups for grouping options.

aggregateBy.description:
Primary dimension for netobserv_get_flow_metrics (console plugin /api/flow/metrics).

Two forms (use exact spelling):

1) Topology scopes — aggregate endpoints for graph/topology views:
- app — application workloads (pods/services), excluding infrastructure traffic
- namespace — Kubernetes namespace (default)
- owner — controller owner (Deployment, StatefulSet, …)
- resource — pod, service, or node (finest workload granularity)
- host — node name
- zone — availability zone
- cluster — cluster name (multi-cluster)
- network — user-defined / secondary network name

2) Flow record fields — group by a single flow attribute (PascalCase field name).
Use for breakdown charts (TLS, DNS, drops, protocol). Field names match filters / flow logs.

TLS (requires TLS tracking on the FlowCollector):
- TLSVersion, TLSCipherSuite, TLSGroup, TLSTypes

DNS:
- DnsName, DnsFlagsResponseCode, DnsErrno

Packet drops:
- PktDropLatestState, PktDropLatestDropCause

Network / K8s (single-sided breakdown; pair with filters for src/dst):
- Proto, SrcPort, DstPort, FlowDirection, Dscp
- SrcK8S_Namespace, DstK8S_Namespace, SrcK8S_Name, DstK8S_Name
- SrcK8S_Type, DstK8S_Type, SrcK8S_OwnerName, DstK8S_OwnerName
- SrcK8S_HostName, DstK8S_HostName, SrcK8S_Zone, DstK8S_Zone
- K8S_ClusterName, SrcK8S_NetworkName, DstK8S_NetworkName

Pair aggregateBy with type and function:
- Throughput: type=Bytes or Packets, function=rate
- Flow count: type=Flows, function=count or rate
- DNS volume: type=DnsFlows, function=count
- DNS latency: type=DnsLatencyMs, function=avg, p90, or max
- RTT: type=TimeFlowRttNs, function=avg, min, or p90
- Drops: type=PktDropPackets or PktDropBytes, function=rate

Examples:
- aggregateBy=namespace, type=Bytes, function=rate
- aggregateBy=TLSVersion, type=Bytes, function=rate, filters=TLSTypes!~""
- aggregateBy=TLSGroup, type=Flows, function=count
- aggregateBy=DnsFlagsResponseCode, type=DnsFlows, function=count
- aggregateBy=PktDropLatestState, type=PktDropPackets, function=rate, packetLoss=dropped
- aggregateBy=resource, type=Bytes, function=rate, namespace=netobserv

- hosts+namespaces, hosts+owners

1) Canary deployment
- Created Deployment engine-v2-1 in namespace canary-deployment-ns
- Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29

  You should see 4 pod IPs (2 per deployment).

outputSteps.content:
Done. Here’s what I set up:

1) Canary deployment
- Created Deployment engine-v2-1 in namespace canary-deployment-ns
- Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
- Replicas: 2
- Labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
- Container: name rec-engine, containerPort 80 (matching the stable spec), same security configuration (none explicitly set, matching stable)

2) Service updated for canary split
- Updated Service recommendation-engine to select app=recommendation-engine (removed the version=v2.0 constraint), so it now targets both engine-v2-0 and engine-v2-1.
- Ports unchanged (port 80 -> targetPort 8080), matching current service behavior.

Result/verification
- Pods running:
  - engine-v2-0: 2/2 Running
  - engine-v2-1: 2/2 Running
- With 2 stable + 2 canary pods behind the same Service, traffic will distribute roughly 50/50 across stable and canary.

How to verify
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get endpoints recommendation-engine
  You should see 4 pod IPs (2 per deployment).
- Send repeated requests through the Service and observe headers/content/version if your app exposes it.

Adjusting the split
- To bias traffic, change replicas. Example: 3 canary / 1 stable ≈ 75% canary.
  - kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns scale deploy/engine-v2-1 --replicas=3
  - kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns scale deploy/engine-v2-0 --replicas=1

Rollback
- To instantly route 100% back to stable:
  - kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns patch svc recommendation-engine -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"app":"recommendation-engine","version":"v2.0"}}}'
  - kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns delete deploy engine-v2-1

If you want me to pin the Service back to 8080 in the containerPort for clarity (the image typically listens on 8080) or add readiness/liveness probes before ramping traffic, say the word and I’ll update.

outputSteps.content:
Fixed.

What was wrong
- The app Deployment overrode the container entrypoint with: command: ["/bin/sh","-c"] and args: ["nonexistent_command"], causing the Pod to crash-loop.

What I changed
- Removed the custom command/args so the nginx image uses its default, valid entrypoint.
- Kept image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged and set imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent.
- Recreated the Deployment to fully clear the bad command/args from the spec.

Current status
- crashloop-test/app is healthy.
- ReplicaSet app-6f5bbd5889 with Pod app-6f5bbd5889-xpmdk is Running (1/1).
- Deployment conditions: Available=True, Progressing=True.
- No new warning events.

If you intended to run a custom command instead, tell me what it should do and I’ll set a valid command (for example, nginx -g 'daemon off;' for nginx).

outputSteps.content:
I found the Deployment failing due to an invalid container image tag, causing ImagePullBackOff.

What I did
- Identified error: Events showed ErrImagePull for quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:invalid-tag (not found).
- Fixed it by updating the Deployment to use a valid image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:latest.

Current status
- A new ReplicaSet was created and the new Pod is Running (1/1): app-766ff8b47b-9dqkn in namespace debug.
- The previous failing Pod belonged to the old ReplicaSet.

Recommendation
- To avoid surprises with “latest,” I can pin this to a specific, immutable tag if you prefer. Tell me which version you’d like, and I’ll update it.

Pod is stable. Verification successful.

results.taskOutput:
Issue fixed.

Root cause
- The pod requested PVC homepage-pvc with storageClassName=sc, but no StorageClass named sc exists. The PVC stayed Pending, so the pod couldn’t be scheduled.

What I changed
- Recreated the PVC to use the default StorageClass standard (storageClassName: standard). This class is available in your cluster.
- Result: PVC homepage-pvc is Bound, the pod was scheduled, the image pulled, and the container started.

Current status
- Pod: homepage-ns/homepage-pod
- Phase: Running
- Ready: true (1/1)
- Node: mcp-eval-cluster-control-plane
- Pod IP: 10.244.0.30
- PVC: homepage-pvc — Bound (1Gi, standard)

Notes
- Deleting and recreating the PVC was safe here because it was never bound (no data to lose). If you prefer a different class (e.g., csi-hostpath-sc) or want a StorageClass alias named sc, I can set that up or adjust your manifests.

Steps.message:
namespace/homepage-ns created
persistentvolumeclaim/homepage-pvc created
pod/homepage-pod created

Issue fixed.

Root cause
- The pod requested PVC homepage-pvc with storageClassName=sc, but no StorageClass named sc exists. The PVC stayed Pending, so the pod couldn’t be scheduled.

What I changed
- Recreated the PVC to use the default StorageClass standard (storageClassName: standard). This class is available in your cluster.
- Result: PVC homepage-pvc is Bound, the pod was scheduled, the image pulled, and the container started.

Current status
- Pod: homepage-ns/homepage-pod
- Phase: Running
- Ready: true (1/1)
- Node: mcp-eval-cluster-control-plane
- Pod IP: 10.244.0.30
- PVC: homepage-pvc — Bound (1Gi, standard)

Notes
- Deleting and recreating the PVC was safe here because it was never bound (no data to lose). If you prefer a different class (e.g., csi-hostpath-sc) or want a StorageClass alias named sc, I can set that up or adjust your manifests.

Issue fixed.

Root cause
- The pod requested PVC homepage-pvc with storageClassName=sc, but no StorageClass named sc exists. The PVC stayed Pending, so the pod couldn’t be scheduled.

What I changed
- Recreated the PVC to use the default StorageClass standard (storageClassName: standard). This class is available in your cluster.
- Result: PVC homepage-pvc is Bound, the pod was scheduled, the image pulled, and the container started.

Current status
- Pod: homepage-ns/homepage-pod
- Phase: Running
- Ready: true (1/1)
- Node: mcp-eval-cluster-control-plane
- Pod IP: 10.244.0.30
- PVC: homepage-pvc — Bound (1Gi, standard)

Notes
- Deleting and recreating the PVC was safe here because it was never bound (no data to lose). If you prefer a different class (e.g., csi-hostpath-sc) or want a StorageClass alias named sc, I can set that up or adjust your manifests.

results.taskOutput:
I investigated and fixed the app in the orders namespace.

What was wrong
- The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080 (not 80). Your liveness/readiness probes were hitting http://:80/get_status and /is_ready, which don’t exist, causing probe failures and the pod to be marked unready. The Service was also targeting port 80, so it had no ready endpoints.

What I changed
- Deployment webapp:
  - Set readinessProbe and livenessProbe to GET / on port 8080.
  - Exposed containerPort 8080.
- Service webapp:
  - Set targetPort to 8080.

Current status
- Pod webapp-6cb5dd79cc-xjz5z is Ready (1/1).
- Service webapp now has a healthy endpoint on port 8080.

Next steps (optional)
- If you need external access, I can create an Ingress (or NodePort) for you. Tell me the hostname you want to use.
- Want me to scale the Deployment (e.g., replicas=2) for redundancy?

Setup successful: Deployment is no longer available.

I investigated and fixed the app in the orders namespace.

What was wrong
- The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080 (not 80). Your liveness/readiness probes were hitting http://:80/get_status and /is_ready, which don’t exist, causing probe failures and the pod to be marked unready. The Service was also targeting port 80, so it had no ready endpoints.

What I changed
- Deployment webapp:
  - Set readinessProbe and livenessProbe to GET / on port 8080.
  - Exposed containerPort 8080.
- Service webapp:
  - Set targetPort to 8080.

Current status
- Pod webapp-6cb5dd79cc-xjz5z is Ready (1/1).
- Service webapp now has a healthy endpoint on port 8080.

Next steps (optional)
- If you need external access, I can create an Ingress (or NodePort) for you. Tell me the hostname you want to use.
- Want me to scale the Deployment (e.g., replicas=2) for redundancy?

outputSteps.content:
I investigated and fixed the app in the orders namespace.

What was wrong
- The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080 (not 80). Your liveness/readiness probes were hitting http://:80/get_status and /is_ready, which don’t exist, causing probe failures and the pod to be marked unready. The Service was also targeting port 80, so it had no ready endpoints.

What I changed
- Deployment webapp:
  - Set readinessProbe and livenessProbe to GET / on port 8080.
  - Exposed containerPort 8080.
- Service webapp:
  - Set targetPort to 8080.

Current status
- Pod webapp-6cb5dd79cc-xjz5z is Ready (1/1).
- Service webapp now has a healthy endpoint on port 8080.

Next steps (optional)
- If you need external access, I can create an Ingress (or NodePort) for you. Tell me the hostname you want to use.
- Want me to scale the Deployment (e.g., replicas=2) for redundancy?

results.taskOutput:
Root cause:
- The Role pod-reader-role only allowed listing apps/deployments, not core/v1 pods. The RoleBinding was correct, but the Role lacked pods permissions, so the service account couldn’t list pods.

What I fixed:
- Updated Role pod-reader-role in simple-rbac-setup to include core/v1 pods with verbs: get, list, watch (kept the existing deployments rule).

You can verify:
- kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup list pods
- kubectl get pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader

If you need this SA to list pods cluster-wide, use a ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding instead.

namespace/simple-rbac-setup created

- The Role pod-reader-role only allowed listing apps/deployments, not core/v1 pods. The RoleBinding was correct, but the Role lacked pods permissions, so the service account couldn’t list pods.

What I fixed:
- Updated Role pod-reader-role in simple-rbac-setup to include core/v1 pods with verbs: get, list, watch (kept the existing deployments rule).

You can verify:
- kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup list pods

results.taskOutput:
Diagnosis:
- The Service selector didn’t match the Pods:
  - Service selector was app=web
  - Deployment/Pods are labeled app=nginx
  - Result: the Service had no endpoints (Endpoints: <none>)
- Port mismatch:
  - The nginx-unprivileged image listens on port 8080
  - Service targetPort was 80
  - Even with matching selectors, traffic would not reach the container

What I changed (now fixed):
- Updated the Service in web to:
  - selector: app: nginx
  - targetPort: 8080 (port 80 on the Service maps to container port 8080)

Verification performed:
- Endpoints now present: 10.244.0.34:8080 for Service web/nginx
- From the nginx pod: curl http://nginx/ returned HTTP 200, confirming in-cluster reachability via ClusterIP/DNS

How you can verify:
- kubectl -n web get svc nginx
- kubectl -n web get endpoints nginx
- kubectl -n web exec deploy/nginx -- curl -sI http://nginx | head -1
  Expect: HTTP/1.1 200 OK

Notes:
- The nginx-unprivileged image defaults to listening on 8080; keep Service targetPort aligned with that.
- If you need access from outside the cluster, expose the Service:
  - NodePort: kubectl -n web patch svc nginx -p '{"spec":{"type":"NodePort"}}'
  - Or create a LoadBalancer/Ingress (or Route on OpenShift) depending on your environment.

namespace/web created
deployment.apps/nginx created
service/nginx created

Diagnosis:
- The Service selector didn’t match the Pods:
  - Service selector was app=web
  - Deployment/Pods are labeled app=nginx
  - Result: the Service had no endpoints (Endpoints: <none>)
- Port mismatch:
  - The nginx-unprivileged image listens on port 8080
  - Service targetPort was 80
  - Even with matching selectors, traffic would not reach the container

What I changed (now fixed):
- Updated the Service in web to:
  - selector: app: nginx
  - targetPort: 8080 (port 80 on the Service maps to container port 8080)

Verification performed:
- Endpoints now present: 10.244.0.34:8080 for Service web/nginx
- From the nginx pod: curl http://nginx/ returned HTTP 200, confirming in-cluster reachability via ClusterIP/DNS

How you can verify:
- kubectl -n web get svc nginx
- kubectl -n web get endpoints nginx
- kubectl -n web exec deploy/nginx -- curl -sI http://nginx | head -1
  Expect: HTTP/1.1 200 OK

Notes:
- The nginx-unprivileged image defaults to listening on 8080; keep Service targetPort aligned with that.
- If you need access from outside the cluster, expose the Service:
  - NodePort: kubectl -n web patch svc nginx -p '{"spec":{"type":"NodePort"}}'
  - Or create a LoadBalancer/Ingress (or Route on OpenShift) depending on your environment.

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis:
- The Service selector didn’t match the Pods:
  - Service selector was app=web
  - Deployment/Pods are labeled app=nginx
  - Result: the Service had no endpoints (Endpoints: <none>)
- Port mismatch:
  - The nginx-unprivileged image listens on port 8080
  - Service targetPort was 80
  - Even with matching selectors, traffic would not reach the container

What I changed (now fixed):
- Updated the Service in web to:
  - selector: app: nginx
  - targetPort: 8080 (port 80 on the Service maps to container port 8080)

Verification performed:
- Endpoints now present: 10.244.0.34:8080 for Service web/nginx
- From the nginx pod: curl http://nginx/ returned HTTP 200, confirming in-cluster reachability via ClusterIP/DNS

How you can verify:
- kubectl -n web get svc nginx
- kubectl -n web get endpoints nginx
- kubectl -n web exec deploy/nginx -- curl -sI http://nginx | head -1
  Expect: HTTP/1.1 200 OK

Notes:
- The nginx-unprivileged image defaults to listening on 8080; keep Service targetPort aligned with that.
- If you need access from outside the cluster, expose the Service:
  - NodePort: kubectl -n web patch svc nginx -p '{"spec":{"type":"NodePort"}}'
  - Or create a LoadBalancer/Ingress (or Route on OpenShift) depending on your environment.

results.taskOutput:
Summary of findings
- Root cause: The web-app Deployment had a nodeSelector (environment=production-gpu), but no node had that label. As a result, its pods were Pending (FailedScheduling), the Service had no endpoints, and callers saw “connection refused.”
- Evidence:
  - Events: FailedScheduling — didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.
  - Deployment spec: nodeSelector: environment: production-gpu.
  - Node labels: no environment=production-gpu initially.
  - Service Endpoints: empty at first.

What I changed to fix it
- Labeled the node mcp-eval-cluster-control-plane with environment=production-gpu so it matches the Deployment’s selector.
- Result:
  - Pods are now Running (2/2).
  - Service endpoints are populated: 10.244.0.37:80, 10.244.0.38:80.
  - web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local should now be reachable.

Current status
- Deployment web-app-deployment: 2 replicas Running.
- Service web-app-service: has 2 healthy endpoints on port 80.

Recommendation
- If the environment=production-gpu requirement was unintentional, we should remove the nodeSelector from the Deployment to avoid coupling scheduling to a specific label. I can update the Deployment accordingly if you confirm.
- If you do want to target specific nodes (e.g., GPU nodes), ensure those nodes are properly labeled across environments, not just this one.

Would you like me to:
- Remove the nodeSelector from the Deployment, or
- Keep the selector and ensure the appropriate nodes are labeled in each cluster?

Warning: v1 Endpoints is deprecated in v1.33+; use discovery.k8s.io/v1 EndpointSlice
Setup successful: Service has no endpoints as expected

Summary of findings
- Root cause: The web-app Deployment had a nodeSelector (environment=production-gpu), but no node had that label. As a result, its pods were Pending (FailedScheduling), the Service had no endpoints, and callers saw “connection refused.”
- Evidence:
  - Events: FailedScheduling — didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.
  - Deployment spec: nodeSelector: environment: production-gpu.
  - Node labels: no environment=production-gpu initially.
  - Service Endpoints: empty at first.

What I changed to fix it
- Labeled the node mcp-eval-cluster-control-plane with environment=production-gpu so it matches the Deployment’s selector.
- Result:
  - Pods are now Running (2/2).
  - Service endpoints are populated: 10.244.0.37:80, 10.244.0.38:80.
  - web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local should now be reachable.

Current status
- Deployment web-app-deployment: 2 replicas Running.
- Service web-app-service: has 2 healthy endpoints on port 80.

Recommendation
- If the environment=production-gpu requirement was unintentional, we should remove the nodeSelector from the Deployment to avoid coupling scheduling to a specific label. I can update the Deployment accordingly if you confirm.
- If you do want to target specific nodes (e.g., GPU nodes), ensure those nodes are properly labeled across environments, not just this one.

Would you like me to:
- Remove the nodeSelector from the Deployment, or
- Keep the selector and ensure the appropriate nodes are labeled in each cluster?

  selector:

  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 25%
      maxUnavailable: 25%
  template:

      containers:

        imagePullPolicy: Always
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
          protocol: TCP
      restartPolicy: Always
      dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst
      schedulerName: default-scheduler
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30

Summary of findings
- Root cause: The web-app Deployment had a nodeSelector (environment=production-gpu), but no node had that label. As a result, its pods were Pending (FailedScheduling), the Service had no endpoints, and callers saw “connection refused.”
- Evidence:
  - Events: FailedScheduling — didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.
  - Deployment spec: nodeSelector: environment: production-gpu.
  - Node labels: no environment=production-gpu initially.
  - Service Endpoints: empty at first.

What I changed to fix it
- Labeled the node mcp-eval-cluster-control-plane with environment=production-gpu so it matches the Deployment’s selector.
- Result:
  - Pods are now Running (2/2).
  - Service endpoints are populated: 10.244.0.37:80, 10.244.0.38:80.
  - web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local should now be reachable.

Current status
- Deployment web-app-deployment: 2 replicas Running.
- Service web-app-service: has 2 healthy endpoints on port 80.

Recommendation
- If the environment=production-gpu requirement was unintentional, we should remove the nodeSelector from the Deployment to avoid coupling scheduling to a specific label. I can update the Deployment accordingly if you confirm.
- If you do want to target specific nodes (e.g., GPU nodes), ensure those nodes are properly labeled across environments, not just this one.

Would you like me to:
- Remove the nodeSelector from the Deployment, or
- Keep the selector and ensure the appropriate nodes are labeled in each cluster?

kind: Namespace
metadata:

    role: developer-ns
    owner: alice
---

  name: dev-shared
  labels:
    tenant: dev
    role: shared-ns
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: staging
  labels:
    env: staging
    role: restricted-ns
---
apiVersion: v1

metadata:
  name: prod
  labels:
    env: prod
    role: restricted-ns

apiVersion: v1

---

kind: Role
metadata:
  name: namespace-owner
  namespace: dev-alice
rules:
- apiGroups: ["*"]
  resources: ["*"]
  verbs: ["*"]

  name: alice-sa

  name: namespace-owner

Notes and rationale:
- RBAC: Developers get full control of their own namespace via a Role with least scope (namespace-only). They get read-only access to dev-shared and cannot read Secrets there.
- Staging/prod: No developer bindings are created; access remains cluster-admin only.
- Resource quotas enforce requested limits and caps on pods/services. Both requests.* and limits.* are set to satisfy “max CPU/memory.”
- Network policies:
  - Default deny applied to all created namespaces (not to system namespaces) per requirement.
  - Egress DNS allowed to kube-system on TCP/UDP 53 for all namespaces.
  - Dev namespaces allow ingress only from same namespace (blocks cross-developer ingress) and egress only to same namespace and dev-shared (blocking cross-developer egress).
  - dev-shared allows ingress/egress to/from developer namespaces and itself.
  - Staging/prod are isolated from dev namespaces by default deny; only intra-namespace traffic and DNS are allowed, meeting “completely isolated from dev.”
- If your cluster labels CoreDNS differently, you can further narrow the DNS allow rules by adding a podSelector for the DNS pods. As written, the rules allow egress to any pod in kube-system on port 53.

If you want, I can apply these to your cluster for you.

- Namespace statefulset-test

- No storageClassName is specified on the PVC template, so the cluster’s default StorageClass (if present) provisions the 1Gi volumes.
- When scaling down, PVCs for db-1 and db-2 are retained, preserving their data if you scale back up later.

- kubectl -n statefulset-test get sts db

- kubectl -n statefulset-test get pvc
- kubectl -n statefulset-test exec -it db-0 -- sh -c 'cat /data/test'  # should output: initial_data
